item.title: Why Myths Still Matter: The Odyssey, the Ego, and the Self
item.description:
Therapy

Why Myths Still Matter: The Odyssey, the Ego, and the Self

How Jung's psychology differentiates ego from self and why it matters in therapy

Posted August 14, 2026

Key points
  • Jung's psychology differentiates between ego and self.
  • A person's ego and self can sometimes be in conflict with each other.
  • Individuation involves reconciliation between ego and self, with the self becoming the personality's center.

In my most recent post on Why Myths Still Matter (here), I was referring to the pivotal point and, for me, most moving scene in Christopher Nolan’s newest film The Odyssey (2026) in which the lost, disoriented, discouraged, delirious, dispirited, defeated, and exhausted hero Odysseus, guided by the goddess Athena (in Jungian terms, representing his own anima or inner feminine), builds a makeshift raft of the remaining broken timbers of his totally wrecked ship, places it in the ocean water, lies down upon it, and surrenders to the natural tides, winds, and currents to take him to his destination. He is a broken, beaten man but finds the inner courage (or desperation) to relinquish control and trust the mysterious power and wisdom of the sea and the gods (the unconscious) rather than continuing to rely on his heroic masculine ego to forcefully and willfully solve the challenge of getting back home to Ithaca.

Dr. Carl Gustav Jung
Source: Wikimedia Commons/Public Domain

The great Swiss psychotherapist Carl Gustav Jung (1955/1963) once pithily commented that “the experience of the Self is always a defeat for the ego.” What he meant is that in order for us to mature and become more whole, balanced, conscious, and authentic (i.e., to individuate), the ego must eventually relinquish its inflated superiority, authority, and megalomaniac illusions regarding its unassailable central and primary place in the psyche and personality.

The ego may indeed be the center of the conscious personality, says Jung (1961), but the self includes, embraces, and incorporates the unconscious as well and stands at the very “centre of this totality.” Our ego, part of the personality which we all have and need, must learn as we mature, usually around midlife or later, to happily and humbly play second fiddle and become subservient and supportive to what Jung (1961) termed the self, by which he meant “the totality of the personality” and its true center.

Sometimes, the ego and self are at odds with each other regarding what we want or need at any given time, but both must be acknowledged and heard. Learning to distinguish, listen to, and honor the essential needs and wants of the self rather than only those of the ego is one of the Herculean labors of mid-life and demands all of our heroic courage, cleverness, commitment, and strength.

Indeed, I prefer to think of this infuriating and humiliating “defeat for the ego” as a traumatic yet potentially transformational process. We, like Odysseus, are insulted, humbled, frustrated, and feel defeated by such untoward events, which can take the form of various outer travails or hardships, apparently impossible situations, enigmatic psychiatric symptoms, and/or unexpected inner crises or conflicts painfully demonstrating that we are not in such complete command of ourselves as we imagined, but are rather subject to the superior or relatively autonomous powers of the unconscious or the daimonic (see Diamond, 1996) and of life itself.

Naturally, the ego furiously resists such realization, displacement, and dethronement, seeking to maintain its illusion of complete control and mastery over inner and outer reality. This powerful resistance on the part of the ego to surrendering to the self is so strong, persistent, and pervasive—and we are so overidentified with our ego or persona, the personification or embodied expression or idealized image of the ego—that sometimes a seemingly insurmountable existential crisis or trauma is required to force our ego down from its narcissistic tower and put it in its proper place. The once proud, omnipotent, and powerful ego must, in the end, accept being subject to the self, not vice versa. Our typical approach to life and problem-solving proves insufficient to solve the crisis now facing us. We must become open and receptive to a new way of seeing and responding to life.

Life inevitably provides precisely that which is called for. A kind of psychological shock therapy. This is one way of thinking about what happens to Odysseus on his own unpredictable odyssey and what happens to each of us on ours. Sometimes, the initial emergence or appearance of the self is experienced as a life-shattering crisis or trauma. When our ego is overwhelmed or thwarted by the superior powers of life or the unconscious, we tend to experience profound depression, grief, confusion, narcissistic injury, anger, resentment, and embitterment. The inflated ego has, despite its best efforts, failed to figure out the problem or solve the puzzle, to find a way to remain in control, to preserve its precious self-importance. But it is precisely in that humiliating defeat and ensuing hopelessness and despair that the unconscious—and specifically what Jung called the psyche’s intrinsic transcendent function—is activated, providing a new and different attitude, insight, approach, or perspective on the problem or seemingly impossible conundrum and how, like the wounded Greek heroes Hercules and Odysseus, to constructively or creatively overcome or resolve it.

Paradoxically, much like Hercules cleaning the Augean stables (see my prior post), this agonizing but necessary “defeat for the ego” clears away accumulated or long-standing obstacles and obstructions, unblocking, purifying, and liberating the life-giving waters of the unconscious self, rendering its revitalizing, renewing, restorative, and creative powers more accessible to us. It is ultimately what, as with Odysseus, makes the successful journey to find and fulfill our destiny possible.

item.title: What Happens When Couples Still Live Together After Breaking Up
item.description:
Relationships

What Happens When Couples Still Live Together After Breaking Up

How to move on when you can't move out.

Posted August 14, 2026

Key points
  • Living with an ex can trigger jealousy, sadness, and confusion.
  • Having feelings after a breakup doesn’t mean ending the relationship was a mistake.
  • Clear boundaries can help you live together without slipping back into being a couple.

In an ideal world, when a relationship comes to an end, you get to pack up your things and go your separate ways. You figure out how to communicate if you have children, but for the most part, you get ample space to create new routines and to process the breakup.

But the world is far from ideal, and breakups are rarely that simple.

Sometimes the relationship ends, but neither one of you can move out. You might own a house or be stuck in a lease together, or perhaps you just don't have enough money to afford two households. There may be children involved, caregiving responsibilities, health concerns, or a hundred other practical reasons why separating your lives isn't as simple as packing a bag and walking out the door.

And how your relationship ends can complicate things even further.

Best-case scenario, you have an honest conversation and agree the relationship has run its course. You’re both sad that it’s over, but there’s no hostility between you. You agree that until one of you can move, you will be roommates.

Or maybe they end things even though you want to keep trying. Now you're sharing a home with someone you still love while trying to accept that they don't want to be with you anymore. Or it might be the other way around: You don't want the relationship anymore, but they don’t want to let you go.

And then there's the breakup that comes after years of fighting, resentment, disappointment, and hurt. You’re both exhausted and completely certain it’s over, but now you have to wake up every morning and see each other.

These situations are completely different. And yet, when you continue living together after a breakup, some surprisingly similar things can happen.

What are they doing?

You might have spent the last six months thinking, I can’t wait to get away from this person. And then one Tuesday evening, you realize they've been on their phone for two hours. Who are they texting? What are they doing?

You essentially ignored them before, but now you're noticing everything: the new clothes they’re wearing, their new gym routine, how often they check their phone.

This can be especially intense when things ended badly. If you’re angry and hurt, you may not want to feel like you’re the only one suffering. You look for signs that they’re hurting too, and when you don’t see them, it infuriates you.

Even in a civil break up, you might be hyperaware of your ex-partner’s comings and goings because sometimes focusing on them feels easier than moving on. As long as you’re wondering what they’re doing, you don’t have to ask yourself the harder question: What am I supposed to do now?

Who are they dating?

Few things will test your belief that you're "doing great" quite like finding out your ex is seeing someone else. This can be incredibly painful when you didn't want things to end, but even when it was a mutual choice or you chose to end it, watching them get ready for a date can feel like emotional whiplash: They're over me already?

There's grief in that, but sometimes there's ego. You may not want them, but that doesn't mean you're ready for them to stop wanting you. Ego in charge, you start doing things to get their attention: looking a little nicer, mentioning your plans, making sure they know you're doing great. Some part of you wants to know that you still matter to them.

What is this sadness?

Sometimes anger carries us through the end of a relationship and even beyond. When there has been a lot of hurt, anger protects us because it keeps all the reasons it needed to end front and center: They were inconsiderate, they were unfaithful, they were selfish. But anger is an emotion, and emotions move. And when anger dissipates, all the other stuff you don’t want to think about or feel takes its place.

Suddenly, memories of the good times begin to surface. You hear them laugh and remember how much you loved that laugh at one point. You see a couple holding hands and remember your first date. You drive past your favorite restaurant and feel the weight of the breakup in ways you hadn’t before.

You’re constantly reminded of happy moments, and you find yourself missing who the two of you used to be before everything went sideways. And try as you might, you can’t access the anger you once felt when you see them standing in the kitchen. All you feel is sadness.

This can be confusing and might lead you to wonder, Why do I miss them? Does this mean I made a mistake?

Not necessarily. Think about when someone dies: They are physically gone, and yet we feel so many emotions long after they took their last breath. It’s no different with a relationship: Putting it to rest doesn’t mean your emotions disappear.

What did we do?!

Intimacy may have been the one thing that kept you feeling connected, especially when the relationship was at its worst. And now you’re broken up, still under the same roof, and both carrying a whole lot of emotions you don’t know what to do with. Before you know it, you’re reaching for what has always felt familiar.

The problem is, the comfort you feel in a moment can create a whole lot of confusion, especially if one of you experiences it as a moment of vulnerability while the other sees it as a sign that maybe it’s not really over.

That's why living together after a breakup requires something you may not have thought to create: intentional boundaries.

3 Ways to Start Moving Forward

Figure out your boundaries. Regardless of how it ended, you need firm boundaries now. Pay attention to what keeps confusing you or pulling you back into the relationship. Maybe it’s sex, asking where they’re going, or just feeling guilty because you ended it. Whatever it is, be honest about whether it’s helping you move on or keeping you stuck.

Get out of their head! Notice how much time you spend wondering what they’re doing, thinking, or feeling. When you catch yourself surfing the waves inside their head, come back to shore: What am I doing? What do I need? What do I want? You don’t have to stop thinking about them; you just need to make more room for you.

Make space for all of it. You can miss them and still know it’s over, feel jealous and know you don’t want them back, love them and know you must let them go. You can know something and feel something completely different at the same time. That’s grief.

Conclusion

Living together after a breakup doesn't have to be messy. It may be awkward, painful, and confusing at times, but with boundaries and a little space, even under the same roof, you can learn how to live with each other without being a couple.
